marks.text: That claim rested heavily on Richard Lee's fieldwork among the Ju/'hoansi (!Kung); Lee's own later accounting, once food processing, tool-making, and housework were included, raised total work closer to a standard industrial week, a revision anthropologists still cite as a caution against the low original estimate. Fieldwork with the Ache of eastern Paraguay directly tested the foraging-versus-farming comparison within a single population: once families that had been full-time foragers settled at an agricultural mission, both men and women worked fewer hours each day than they had in the forest, ate less, and shifted their childcare and labor patterns.
marks.reason: The passage directly supports the claim that Ache men and women worked fewer hours each day after settling at an agricultural mission compared to when they were foragers.

partial_support.reason: The passage does not mention Richard Lee's fieldwork among the Ju/'hoansi (!Kung) or his later accounting of work hours.

marks.text: Consistent with this, a study of the Agta of the Philippines found individuals in camps more engaged in agricultural and other non-foraging work had substantially less leisure, a difference driven mainly by women's changing time use.
marks.reason: The passage directly states that the negative relationship between leisure time and engagement in non-foraging out-of-camp work is driven largely by women, who spent less time at leisure in camps more heavily engaged in agriculture and other non-foraging work.
